new_statements.quote: [p.30, sec. 3.6] Basically, the primary stress in any word falls on the first syllable, with secondary stress on the third syllable of a four-syllable root or a trisyllabic word carrying a monosyllabic suffix and/or on the first syllable of any bound disyllabic morpheme, or on the first of a pair of bound monosyllabic morphemes if it does not tend to form a diphthong or long vowel with the preceding vowel (i.e. is not -yi after /a/ or /i/). ... Secondary stresses are not always detectable. [p.7, sec. 1.5] Clearly only one language is involved ... There are very few and only sporadic phonological differences between the dialects; the most salient involves a group of words beginning with /y/ in Yandruwandha and /tj/ in Yawarrawarrka

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the first syllable. Secondary stress is largely morphology-driven: on the initial syllable of bound disyllabic morphemes, on the 3rd syllable of four-syllable roots (or trisyllabic word + monosyllabic suffix), or on the first of two bound monosyllables unless it coalesces with the preceding vowel. Stated for Yandruwandha as a whole, which for Breen includes Yawarrawarrka as a dialect with no reported prosodic differences.
new_statements.secondary_stress: On 3rd syllable of a four-syllable root or trisyllabic word + monosyllabic suffix; on first syllable of any bound disyllabic morpheme; on first of a pair of bound monosyllabic suffixes (unless -yi after a/i); alternative: secondary on a monosyllabic suffix preceding a disyllabic one; non-productive stem formatives count as part of the root; 'Secondary stresses are not always detectable'; a common deviation is secondary stress on the 2nd syllable of a trisyllable (p.32).
new_statements.exceptions: Grammatical words (pronouns, auxiliaries) may occur without primary stress; a primary stress on a grammatical word may transfer to the last syllable of the preceding word (two primary stresses); ngaandi 'yes' has an abnormal pattern [ŋaándi]; compound nouns alternate between one-word (primary+secondary) and two-word (two primaries) stressing; 'Other deviations from the standard are not uncommon but may be random and unmotivated' (p.32).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress (sec. 3.6) distinguished explicitly from 'phrase stress' (sec. 3.6.1), whose position is unpredictable and may fall on syllables that carry no word stress. Description based mainly on Innamincka Yandruwandha speakers (Kerwin, Guttie); Yawarrawarrka material (Naylon, Harris brothers) is included in the corpus but the stress section does not single it out. Innamincka Words (PL 559) p.5 restates: 'The main stress (or accent) in Yandruwandha words is on the first syllable.'
new_statements.identity_note: The only description is Breen 2004 'Innamincka Talk', whose object language is Yandruwandha, principally the Innamincka dialect (Glottolog yand1253). Breen treats Yawarrawarrka as a dialect of the same language ('Clearly only one language is involved', p.7) and includes Yawarrawarrka data (from Maudie Naylon, the Harris/Harrison brothers, Reuther) throughout as 'notes on other dialects'. The stress statement in sec. 3.6 is made for the language as a whole with no Yawarrawarrka-specific qualification; p.7 states 'There are very few and only sporadic phonological differences between the dialects', the ones listed being segmental (y/tj word-initially). Glottolog splits Yawarawarga off as its own languoid yawa1258; the catalog already holds yand1253 from the same section, so this entry would be a dialect-level extension of that record, not an independent description.

sources.note: Sec. 3.6 (pp.30-32): primary stress on the first syllable of any word; secondary stress on 3rd syllable of a four-syllable root (or trisyllable + monosyllabic suffix) and/or first syllable of bound disyllabic morphemes; secondary stresses not always detectable; grammatical words may lack primary stress; ngaandi 'yes' abnormal; 3.6.1 phrase stress unpredictable in position. No separate statement for Yawarrawarrka; p.7 says only one language is involved and phonological differences between dialects are 'very few and only sporadic' (segmental y/tj).
Nothing; bibliography gives only Breen 2004 as descriptive reference (plus Breen 2007, Bowern 2010, Bowern & Atkinson 2012 for classification).
